text: Loops over candidates, and shrinking the search space.
**Enumeration** tries every candidate and keeps the ones that pass a test. It is always correct if the list is complete, so the only question is speed. Count the candidates before you code.

title: How big is the search space?
rows: k choices in each of n places

text: Three ways to make enumeration fast enough: enumerate **fewer variables** and compute the last one; **tighten the bounds** of each loop; **change what you enumerate**.
Counting rectangles by their two corners is O(n²m²). A block of height h and width w fits in (n − h + 1)(m − w + 1) places, so enumerate the **size** instead.
Enumerating sizes is O(nm): 25 million steps for 5000 × 5000 (P2241).
Choosing all nine digits is 9! = 362 880 arrangements. Once the first number x is known, the ratio fixes the other two, so only about 900 values of x need testing (P1618).
A `bool seen[10]` array checks "each digit once" in one pass.
For A + B = C only A and B are free: C = A + B. With at most 24 sticks every number stays below about 1111, so two loops of about 1100 suffice (P1149).
Get the bound from the limits, then test it: a bigger bound must not change any answer. More practice: P3392, P3654, P3799.
Every subset by binary masks, and by choose or skip recursion.
A set of n items has 2ⁿ subsets. Number them 0 … 2ⁿ − 1 and read each in binary: **bit i is 1 when item i is chosen**. One loop visits every subset once.
Test bit i with `mask >> i & 1`. `1 << n` is 2ⁿ. n ≤ 20 gives about a million subsets.
PERKET (P2036) needs every non empty subset, so the loop starts at mask 1. "Choose exactly k" (P1036) keeps only masks with k bits set.

title: Subsets by recursion: choose or skip

text: Each level decides one item: **take** it, recurse, then **undo** and try the next. Taking only later numbers lists every combination once, in dictionary order (P1157).
Take, recurse, undo is the heart of backtracking (chapter 14).
Every ordering with next_permutation, and by recursion with pruning.
A permutation is an ordering of all n items; there are n! (10! = 3 628 800). `next_permutation` steps to the next ordering in dictionary order.
It returns false after the largest ordering. Starting unsorted skips every smaller ordering: **sort first**, and use do … while so the first one prints too (P1706).
Adding m to a permutation is m steps of next_permutation (P1088).
Fill the positions one at a time; `used[v]` remembers which values are taken. The recursive form can **prune**: stop a branch as soon as it breaks a rule.
Ten ingredients of 1, 2 or 3 grams adding up to n: at most 3¹⁰ = 59 049 recipes. If even all 1s left would exceed n, or all 3s could not reach it, stop that branch (P2089).
